newsitem.title: USA: Mexico pins hopes on new social security system.
newsitem.headline: Mexico pins hopes on new social security system.

text.p: Mexico expects its new social security system to raise between $3 and $4 billion next year when it starts operating, Mexican officials said Wednesday.
Using what they termed conservative projections, the Mexican officials said the social security system could accumulate the equivalent of 40 percent of Mexico's GDP in 20 or 25 years' time.
"This is important because this is the first time that Mexico will have a long-term capital market," Mexican Finance Secretary Guillermo Ortiz said at a news conference.
Clearly warming to the topic, Ortiz ignored an aide's suggestion to wrap up the briefing and went on to explain why the social security reform was so important for Mexico.
"Mexico has never had the chance to finance projects over 20 or 30 years with domestic savings," he noted.
The Mexican government decided last year to switch from a pay-as-you-go state-run pensions system to one styled after Chile's hugely successful individual savings accounts scheme.
The Chilean system, where workers' pension savings are managed by private sector funds, has accumulated in 15 years more than 40 percent of that country's GDP.

Those savings allowed Chile to virtually insulate itself from Mexico's peso crisis. While neighboring Argentina, which lacked such a buffer, fell into a recession, Chile's GDP grew 8.5 percent last year.

The president of Mexico's National Commission for the Pensions Savings System (CONSAR), Fernando Sols Sobern, said at the same news conference that the forecasts for the Mexican accumulation of savings depended on the level of wages and employment, on how much workers saved of their salaries, as well as of the yields eventually obtained on investments.

As for the existing 1.5 million pensioners, the Mexican government will start paying their pensions. Sols said that outlay would represent a cost of around 0.2 percent of GDP, or $700 million next year.

Those expenditures would continue to increase gradually until they reach about 0.5 percent of GDP in the year 2020, when they should begin to decline as the population of pensioners covered under the old system decreases.
